blocks.text: A program that returns the expected answer on one example has demonstrated one observation. An algorithm becomes dependable when its input domain, state transitions, invariants, output guarantees, and resource costs can be explained together. This volume develops that discipline through complete C++ implementations rather than treating data structures as names to memorize or code to copy without understanding.

blocks.text: The original twenty-chapter curriculum is preserved, including all forty numbered sections and eighty numbered subsections. The expanded explanations connect abstract reasoning to object lifetime, ownership, failure handling, tests, and the memory behavior of actual programs. Every chapter retains a complete worked program and adds deeper traces, failure investigation, guided practice, and solution reasoning. The appendices supply additional executable laboratories and an integrated routing application that combines several of the book’s techniques.

topics.title: Audience and progression
topics.summary: This book assumes the C++ fundamentals and resource-management concepts taught in Books I and II. You should be able to read functions, classes, standard containers, references, smart pointers, lambdas, and basic templates. The common language baseline is C++20. The book does not require competitive-programming experience or an advanced mathematics background, but it asks you to follow precise arguments and to distinguish examples from proofs.

blocks.text: Chapters 1 and 2 establish contracts, invariants, and complexity. Chapters 3–12 examine sequence, associative, hierarchical, and priority structures. Chapters 13–19 develop graph traversal, searching, sorting, recursion, greedy reasoning, and dynamic programming. Chapter 20 connects these abstractions to measurement on real hardware. The supplementary application is best read after graph traversal, heaps, and algorithmic correctness are familiar.

blocks.text: The custom containers deliberately have narrower contracts than their standard-library counterparts. An integer-only dynamic array is not a drop-in std::vector; a fixed open-addressing table is not a general std::unordered_map; a color-property checker is not a complete red-black tree implementation. These boundaries are stated where they matter. Standard containers remain the default practical choice unless a measured requirement justifies specialized storage.

topics.title: Technical scope and evidence
topics.summary: The examples use standard C++20 and the standard library, with CMake and Python for building and fixture execution. The companion does not download third-party C++ dependencies. Language references point to the C++20 working draft N4861 rather than silently applying a future draft to the selected baseline. Compiler and build-tool documentation is separate because tool options and diagnostics can change independently of the language standard.

topics.title: Read for a decision, then trace the mechanism
topics.summary: Begin each example by stating the required result and the accepted input domain. Then identify the representation and the invariant that gives its fields meaning. Trace one small success, one boundary, and one failure before studying performance. This sequence prevents a fast but incorrectly modeled implementation from becoming the baseline.

blocks.text: Read the text between code blocks. It explains assumptions that a short listing cannot express by syntax alone: whether duplicates are allowed, whether an index is borrowed from a mutable sequence, whether a graph is directed, whether a result is one of several optima, and what remains unchanged after an operation fails. Those decisions determine which tests are meaningful.

blocks.text: The recurring working rule is: define the contract, preserve the invariant, verify the result, and measure only the work you intend to compare. In a proof, identify initialization, preservation, and termination. In a test, identify setup, action, and observation. In a benchmark, identify preparation, timed work, and result consumption.

topics.title: Practice without confusing failure with corruption
topics.summary: Use a separate experimental copy when deliberately breaking an invariant. Many mistakes can be demonstrated safely by returning a wrong value, rejecting a valid input, or omitting a necessary update. Do not invoke undefined behavior merely to create a dramatic example. A dangling reference does not become a legitimate experiment because it happened to print a familiar value once.
